questions.stem: Dandelion fruits have a parachute-like structure of fine hairs. A student observes that dandelion seeds can travel several kilometres from the parent plant. What is the main advantage of this dispersal method?

options.text: It ensures all seeds land in the same area for safety
It reduces competition between seedlings and the parent plant for light, water, and minerals
It protects the seeds from being eaten by animals
It means the seeds will germinate faster in new locations

questions.explanation: Dispersing seeds far from the parent plant reduces competition for resources such as light, water, and soil minerals. If all seeds fell directly beneath the parent, they would compete with each other and with the established parent plant, reducing their chances of survival. Wind dispersal spreads seeds over a wide area, colonising new habitats.

questions.stem: Blackberry fruits are brightly coloured and contain sugary flesh surrounding the seeds. The seeds have a tough outer coat that resists digestion. How does this combination of features aid dispersal?

options.text: The bright colour warns animals that the fruit is poisonous
Animals eat the fruit for its sweet flesh, and the tough seeds pass through the digestive system unharmed, being deposited far away in droppings
The seeds are dispersed by wind because the fruit is lightweight
The sugary flesh feeds the seed as it germinates inside the animal

questions.explanation: This is an example of animal dispersal. Bright colour and sweet flesh attract animals to eat the fruit. The seeds have a tough, indigestible coat that protects them as they pass through the animal's gut. The seeds are deposited in the animal's droppings, often far from the parent plant, along with a natural supply of fertiliser.

questions.stem: Coconut fruits have a thick fibrous husk and can float on seawater for months. Which type of dispersal does this represent, and why is it effective?

options.text: Wind dispersal; the husk acts like a parachute
Animal dispersal; animals carry coconuts to new locations
Water dispersal; the waterproof husk allows the coconut to float across oceans and colonise new coastlines
Explosive dispersal; the husk bursts open to scatter seeds

questions.explanation: Coconuts are dispersed by water. The thick, fibrous, waterproof husk contains air spaces that make the coconut buoyant. It can float across oceans for months without the seed being damaged by saltwater. When it washes ashore, the seed can germinate on new coastlines. This explains how coconut palms colonised tropical islands.

questions.stem: Burdock fruits have tiny hooks on their surface. A dog walker notices these fruits clinging to their dog's fur after a walk. Why is the hook structure an effective adaptation for dispersal?

options.text: The hooks protect the seeds from being eaten by predators
The hooks anchor the seed to the soil for germination
The hooks attach to animal fur or clothing, carrying seeds to new locations before falling off
The hooks help the fruit catch the wind for wind dispersal

questions.explanation: Burdock fruits are dispersed by animals through external attachment. The tiny hooks catch on animal fur (or human clothing), and the fruit is carried to a new location. Eventually the fruit falls off, depositing the seeds far from the parent plant. This method inspired the invention of Velcro.

questions.stem: Himalayan balsam pods explode when ripe, shooting seeds up to 7 metres away. A student argues this is the most effective dispersal method. What is a valid limitation of explosive dispersal compared to other methods?

options.text: Seeds are damaged by the force of the explosion
Seeds can only travel a short distance, so they may still face competition near the parent plant compared to wind or animal dispersal
The explosion kills the parent plant, so it cannot reproduce again
Explosive dispersal only works in wet conditions

questions.explanation: While explosive (self) dispersal can propel seeds several metres, this distance is relatively short compared to wind dispersal (which can carry seeds kilometres) or animal dispersal (which can transport seeds even further). Seeds landing close to the parent still face competition for resources, though explosive dispersal does spread them beyond the immediate vicinity.
